```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

Regular grids have the same relative distances around every focal location.
The default `search = "auto"` selects grid offsets for sufficiently occupied
regular lattices and for constructed grid/pycnophylactic surfaces. Other inputs
use brute force for radius neighborhoods and boost for population-based kNN.
Explicit `search = "grid"`, `"brute"`, or `"boost"` selects a backend directly.

`search = "grid"` exploits this structure by preparing an ordered set of cell
offsets once. For radius neighborhoods, it also prepares the spatial weights
once for each bandwidth. This approach follows the grid-offset principle used
by [EquiPop](https://www.uu.se/en/department/human-geography/research/equipop)
(Osth, 2014; Osth, Clark, and Malmberg, 2015,
[doi:10.1111/gean.12053](https://doi.org/10.1111/gean.12053)).

## Agents on a grid

Each row here represents an agent at a grid location. Group A occupies one side
of the square and group B the other.

```{r agents}
library(segcetera)
library(ggplot2)

agents <- expand.grid(x = 0:9, y = 0:9)
agents$group <- ifelse(agents$x + agents$y < 9, "A", "B")
variables <- list(group = seg_categorical("group"))

result <- seg_measure(
  agents,
  variables,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  bands = c(0, 2, 4),
  search = "auto",
  grid_size = 1,
  output = "full"
)
as.data.frame(result)
result$neighbors$engine
```

The cell size is one coordinate unit in both directions. With complete regular
axes, `grid_size` can also be inferred. Specifying the known spacing is useful
when cells are absent or coordinates have large offsets, as with projected maps.

```{r local-environments}
environments <- as.data.frame(result, what = "env")
environments$x <- agents$x[environments$location]
environments$y <- agents$y[environments$location]

ggplot(subset(environments, category == "A"), aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), name = "Group A\nshare") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()
```

Missing cells contribute zero population. Multiple agents can occupy the same
cell, and remain separate observations in the output. The grid has finite
boundaries: offsets extending beyond it are skipped. Results are returned for
the supplied focal rows.

## Comparing searches

The grid backend uses the same neighborhood and index definitions as the
general-coordinate backends. Here the indices and local environments agree.

```{r compare-backends}
reference <- seg_measure(
  agents, variables, coords = c("x", "y"), bands = c(0, 2, 4),
  search = "brute", output = "full"
)
isTRUE(all.equal(result$analyses, reference$analyses, tolerance = 1e-12))
result$diagnostics$grid
```

The diagnostics report the grid dimensions and origin, the number of prepared
offsets, and the number of cached weights. Offsets at equal distances share a
weight, reducing the cache size. The offset and weight cache has a 512 MiB
budget. A request exceeding it raises an error; smaller radius bands or a
different search backend can then be used.

## Rectangular cells and population thresholds

Use two cell dimensions for rectangular spacing. Population-based nearest
neighborhoods use the same offset ordering, stopping when the requested eligible
population is reached. Tied boundary populations are included proportionately.
Their adaptive kernel weights are calculated for each neighborhood.

```{r rectangular-knn}
rectangular <- transform(agents, x = 2 * x, y = 3 * y)
nearest <- seg_measure(
  rectangular,
  variables,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  neighbors = "knn",
  bands = c(5, 20),
  search = "grid",
  grid_size = c(2, 3)
)
as.data.frame(nearest)
```

For polygon inputs, `surface = "grid"` or `surface = "pycno"` first constructs
a population surface. Combining either with `search = "grid"` automatically uses
the generated cell dimensions. `surface` controls the population representation;
`search` controls how neighborhoods are calculated.

The grid backend is most useful when a reasonably dense regular lattice is
shared by many focal locations. Sparse grids with many empty positions may
favor `search = "boost"`. Runtime also depends on the largest neighborhood and
the variables being analyzed.
